questions.text: What does Bubble Sort compare?
options: Neighbouring elements, two at a time
The first element with the last
Each element with the biggest one
Each element with every other one

questions.text: When do two neighbours swap, to sort from smallest to largest?
options: When the right one is bigger
When the left one is bigger
When they are equal
When the left one is the biggest of all

questions.text: After the first pass, where is the biggest number?
options: At the start
In the middle
At the end
Where it was

questions.text: Why is it called Bubble Sort?
options: Each pass, the smallest number left bubbles up to the start
Each pass, the first number bubbles all the way to the end
Each pass, the biggest number left bubbles up to the start
Each pass, the biggest number left bubbles up to the end

questions.text: What does `a, b = b, a` do?
options: It swaps the values of a and b
It sets both a and b to the value of b
It copies a into b and leaves a as it was
It stops with an error

questions.text: Which line swaps numbers[j] and numbers[j + 1]?
options: numbers[j], numbers[j + 1] = numbers[j], numbers[j + 1]
numbers[j], numbers[j + 1] = numbers[j + 1], numbers[j]
numbers[j], numbers[j + 1] = numbers[j + 1], numbers[j + 1]
numbers[j], numbers[j + 1] == numbers[j + 1], numbers[j]

questions.text: Why does j go only up to len(numbers) - 1?
options: Because the last element is already in place before any pass
To make it faster, since the last pair never needs a swap
Because j is compared with j + 1, which must stay in the list
To make each pass one step shorter than the pass before it

questions.text: What does the outer loop (i) count?
options: Which pair of neighbours is compared
The swaps made in the list
The index of the biggest number
The passes over the list

questions.text: What does the inner loop (j) do?
options: It walks the list and compares each pair of neighbours
It counts how many passes the list still needs
It compares each element with the first one
It sorts the whole list by itself in a single pass

questions.text: At most how many passes does a list of n elements need?
options: n
n × n

questions.text: Roughly how many comparisons does Bubble Sort make for n elements?
options: About n
About n / 2
About n × n
About n + n

questions.text: About how many comparisons for 10 elements?
Is Bubble Sort a good choice for a million numbers?
options: No: about a million million comparisons, very slow
Yes: about a million comparisons, one per number
Yes: it is as fast as sorted() on lists of any size
No: about two million comparisons, two per number

questions.text: What do we use to sort in real code?
options: Bubble Sort, since it is the simplest
sorted(), with a faster algorithm
min() in a loop, one number at a time
Bubble Sort for numbers, sorted() for words

questions.text: Why learn Bubble Sort then?
options: Because it is faster than sorted() when the list is short
Because sorted() changes the list, while Bubble Sort leaves it alone
It teaches comparisons and swaps, which many algorithms build on
Because most real code still sorts big lists with Bubble Sort

questions.text: In [5, 3, 8, 1, 2], what is the list after the first comparison?
In [3, 5, 8, 1, 2], 5 and 8 are compared. What happens?
options: They stay: 5 is smaller
They swap: 8 is bigger
8 moves straight to the end
The pass stops: they are in order

questions.text: What is [5, 3, 8, 1, 2] after the first pass?
What does ascending order mean?
options: From largest to smallest
Only in alphabetical order
From smallest to largest
In the order the items were added

questions.text: How do you make Bubble Sort sort from largest to smallest?
options: Make j go from the end of the list to the start
Swap when the left one is bigger, as before
Add reverse=True, as with sorted()
Swap when the left one is smaller: use <

questions.text: What does Bubble Sort change in a list that is already sorted?
options: Nothing: no pair needs to swap
It reverses it into descending order
It swaps every pair of neighbours once
It stops with an error: nothing to sort

Return the sorted list

Return how many elements it has

options: The smallest two, at the start
Only the biggest one, at the end
None yet: that takes n passes
The biggest two, at the end

questions.text: What happens if j reaches the last index and the code reads numbers[j + 1]?
options: It stops with an IndexError
It reads the first element
It reads 0
Nothing, the line is skipped

questions.text: What would a swap need in many other languages?
options: A second list to copy the values into
A temporary variable to hold one value
An if to check which value is bigger
Nothing more: the same one-line swap

questions.text: Does the lesson's Bubble Sort change the list or make a new one?
options: It makes a new list and leaves the old one as it was
It makes a new copy of the list on each pass
It changes the same list, swapping inside it
